# Human migrations: sources and route notes

Research checked September 21, 2026. Story copy is in `tour-stories.md`; the geographic route data is in `tour-migrations.mjs`.

## Reading the map

This is an editorial overview of selected **Homo sapiens** dispersals, inspired by Alexandre Van de Sande’s [World map of prehistoric human migrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_human_migrations#/media/File:World_map_of_prehistoric_human_migrations.jpg). It is not a reproduction of that map’s mitochondrial haplogroup tree. It does not include the much earlier expansions of Homo erectus, every subsequent migration, or all movement back into Africa.

The waypoint coordinates are an illustrative synthesis, not a published GPS dataset. Lines indicate broad connections, not known footpaths. Branches are oriented away from their junctions to make the map readable; moving dots do not measure travel speed, date, population size, or ancestry proportions. The color groups overlap in time and are not three discrete, universally agreed migration events.

Present-day coastlines are retained. Ice-age Beringia, Sunda and Sahul included land now underwater, while crossings through Wallacea still required travel by sea. Geographic cuts in the hexagonal map interrupt lines; they do not imply interrupted migrations.

## African origins and early departures

- Earlier human relatives also dispersed from Africa. [Smithsonian: Homo erectus](https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-erectus) documents its presence across Africa and western and eastern Asia. The broad geographic overlap with later Homo sapiens dispersals does not establish identical tracks, departure points or destinations; the plotted lines remain specific to the Homo sapiens overview.
- [Smithsonian: Ancient DNA and Neanderthals](https://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/genetics/ancient-dna-and-neanderthals) describes Neanderthals evolving outside Africa and interbreeding with Homo sapiens. Their deeper ancestry connects to earlier African populations, but Neanderthals were not simply another wave of our species leaving the same East African location. They contributed ancestry to many living people through interbreeding.
- [Ragsdale et al., Nature (2023): A weakly structured stem for human origins in Africa](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06055-y). Supports long interaction among ancestral African populations. The East African marker is a narrative anchor, not evidence that all modern humans originated at that coordinate. The map does not turn this population model into invented intra-African migration tracks.
- [Hershkovitz et al., Science (2018): The earliest modern humans outside Africa](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29371468/). Misliya’s upper jaw was dated to about 177,000–194,000 years ago. The early Levant branch also represents repeated occupation, rather than one journey lasting 100,000 years.
- [Abbas et al., Science Advances (2023): Human dispersals out of Africa via the Levant](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10550223/). Wetland evidence supports the Levant as a viable dispersal corridor during wetter phases. The early northern branch encompasses the familiar Skhul/Qafzeh evidence around 120,000–90,000 years ago.
- [Groucutt et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2018): Homo sapiens in Arabia by 85,000 years ago](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41559-018-0518-2). The Al Wusta fossil supports early Arabian occupation. Its drawn connection to the Levant is schematic, not a demonstrated individual itinerary.

## Eurasia: several lines of evidence, different clocks

- [Nature (2025): Major expansion in the human niche preceded out of Africa dispersal](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09154-0). Finds ecological expansion within Africa from around 70,000 years ago, peaking around 50,000 years ago in association with successful later dispersals.
- [Vallini et al., Nature Communications (2024): The Persian plateau served as hub for Homo sapiens after the main out of Africa dispersal](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-46161-7). A model identifying the plateau as a likely population hub. This motivates the southwest Asian junction, whose exact position is an editorial choice. Neither the northern exit nor the Bab el-Mandeb alternative is presented as the uniquely proven route.
- [Sümer et al., Nature (online 2024; volume 2025): Earliest modern human genomes constrain timing of Neanderthal admixture](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08420-x). Genomes from Ranis and Zlatý kůň inform early European population history and estimate shared Neanderthal admixture around 45,000–49,000 years ago. This constrains genetic histories; it does not directly date every exit from Africa. Its implications are in tension with some earlier Sahul chronologies, which remain visible as uncertainty here.
- [Nature Communications (2024): Environmental conditions associated with initial northern expansion of anatomically modern humans](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-48762-8). Environmental modeling informs broad connections across Eurasia, Siberia and toward Beringia/Japan. The drawn curves are illustrative, not extracted model trajectories.

## Sahul: two proposed approaches

- [Gandini et al., Science Advances (2025): Genomic evidence supports the “long chronology” for the peopling of Sahul](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12662211/). A mitochondrial study supports settlement around 60,000 years ago and possible northern and southern entries, via the Sulawesi/Moluccas region and Flores/Timor respectively. These are model-supported alternatives, not settled tracks. Molecular-clock assumptions and incomplete sampling matter; shorter chronologies remain part of the debate.
- [Clarkson et al., Nature (2017): Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature22968). Madjedbebe provides archaeological support for an early arrival; the age and its relationship to genetic estimates remain debated.
- [Tobler et al., Nature (2017): Aboriginal mitogenomes reveal 50,000 years of regionalism in Australia](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature21416). Supports early differentiation and dispersal down eastern and western Australia, reaching the south around 49,000–45,000 years ago. These branches are a broad summary, not precise routes for individual communities.

## The Americas: early presence and repeated dispersals

- [Willerslev & Meltzer, Nature (2021): Peopling of the Americas as inferred from ancient genomics](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03499-y). Genetic synthesis informing the Beringian connection and subsequent differentiation. Coastal and interior corridors have different histories; the ice-free interior route is shown as later movement, not an explanation for the oldest southern evidence.
- [USGS, Fact Sheet 2025-3046: Fossil footprints and Ice Age ecosystems of White Sands National Park](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/fs20253046/full). Documents human presence around 23,000–21,000 years ago. The route to White Sands is unknown; the short illustrated branch is only a geographic connection. Do not equate the date of these footprints with a proven date for one particular coastal migration.
- [Nature Communications (2025): Climate influence on the early human occupation of South America during the late Pleistocene](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-58134-5). Finds evidence of early western/Andean dispersal and later eastward occupation patterns in the south. This informs the Andean trunk and eastward branch, rather than depicting settlement solely along the coast.
- [The evolutionary history and unique genetic diversity of Indigenous Americans, Nature (2026)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10406-w). Reports evidence for at least three principal population dispersals into South America, including turnover from around 9,000 years ago and a further later component. These are inferred population histories, not three recovered geographic tracks. One additional schematic branch signals repeated movement without assigning unsupported paths or exact dates to each ancestry component.

## Deliberate limits

The main 70,000–40,000-year color band is an orientation aid, not a reconciliation of every chronology. European genome-based dates and the long Sahul chronology should not be forced into a single precise departure date. Similarly, early American archaeological presence does not by itself settle the route or its genetic relationships.

Later Austronesian and Polynesian voyages have their own discovery point. Farming expansions, Bantu migrations, later Arctic dispersals and historical migrations are outside this first overview. The data structure keeps stable route IDs, source keys, evidence periods and uncertainty notes so these can be expanded without replacing the rendering system.
